t: Maximum Value Sum by Placing Three Rooks II
o: Place 3 non-attacking rooks (distinct rows and columns) maximizing the sum of covered cells; values may be negative but exactly 3 rooks are required. Key fact: in an optimal placement, each rook's cell is among the top-4 values of its row (the other two rooks eliminate at most 2 columns). Enumerate the middle row and combine precomputed top candidates from rows above and below.
k: Each chosen cell is within the top-4 of its row and top-4 of its column — at most 2 columns are blocked by the other rooks.

Enumerate the middle row b (by row index) and its column from its top-4; merge top candidates from rows < b and rows > b (filtered to exclude b's column), then try all cross pairs checking column distinctness.
Incremental merging of per-row top-4 lists keeps the whole algorithm near O(m·k²).

a.n: Approach 1: Middle-Row Enumeration with Top-k Candidates
a.i: Every valid triple of rows has a middle row b. For fixed b and b's column jb, the best rook above uses one of the top-3 values among rows < b excluding column jb (its own exclusion of one more column is covered by taking 3 candidates), likewise below; testing all 3×3 pairs with a column-equality check finds the optimum.
s: Build leftTop[b] = merged top-6 of rows < b incrementally; rightTop[b] similarly from the bottom.
For each b and each of its top-4 cells (vb, jb): filter side lists to columns ≠ jb, take top-3 each, try all pairs with distinct columns, update the answer.
a.t: O(m·n + m²·k²) with k = 4 — the per-middle-row candidate gathering dominates at O(m²)

w: The top-4-per-row argument is the crux — articulate it clearly (two other rooks block at most two columns). Pitfalls: negative values mean you cannot skip 'bad' cells; exactly 3 rooks must be placed; column-distinctness must be checked between the outer pair too. Follow-up: generalize to k rooks — the same top-(k+1) candidate argument extends recursively.
